challenges.headline: Invoice issued on signature
challenges.premise: The invoice should be created automatically at the moment of signature, as if one signature meant one invoice.
challenges.alternative: Create a draft invoice at signature and let a billing user validate it before it is numbered and issued. Alternatively, generate invoices from a billing schedule anchored on the contract start date or milestones.
challenges.consequence: A legally numbered invoice is hard to undo. An amendment re-signing, a revoked signature or incomplete contract data would produce wrong invoices, credit notes and gaps in the sequential numbering.
challenges.recommendation: Agree with Finance that the automation produces drafts, and issuance remains a deliberate step, at least for the first release.

challenges.headline: One invoice per contract
challenges.premise: A signed contract maps to a single invoice created in one go.
challenges.alternative: Model the contract as owning a billing schedule (single, milestones, recurring, partial) and let the signature activate that schedule, rather than emit one document.
challenges.consequence: If contracts really bill in several instalments, a one-invoice hook is thrown away and rebuilt, and any billing-rule change must ripple across every invoice the contract emits.
challenges.recommendation: Review a sample of real signed contracts to see how many invoices each actually yields before sizing the work.

challenges.headline: Build before checking existing tools
challenges.premise: The right answer is to build new automation in the platform.
challenges.alternative: First check whether the existing invoicing module, an accounting or billing tool already paid for, or an unused automation feature covers part of this.
challenges.consequence: Building something that already exists wastes effort and adds a second path to maintain.
challenges.recommendation: Spend a short audit on existing licensed features and tools before committing build effort.

page.title: Automatic invoicing on contract signature
page.recommendation: Decide whether signature should create a draft invoice for review or a final, numbered one. We recommend automating creation of draft invoices from the signature event, with protection against duplicates and a visible queue for contracts with missing data. Issuing stays a deliberate step for now.
page.why: Your request names the trigger but not the need behind it, how many invoices a contract produces, or what happens when data is missing. An issued invoice is legally numbered and hard to undo, so starting with drafts lets you gain the time saving while keeping a safety net. It also avoids committing to a billing engine before we know how your contracts actually bill.
page.cost_and_risk: The main cost is the rule set that turns a contract into one or several invoices: amount source, VAT, payment terms and numbering. The risk that matters most is duplicate or wrong invoices, for example when an amendment is signed again and re-triggers the automation.

challenges.headline: One invoice per signature
challenges.premise: Signing a contract produces a single invoice, so the automation is a simple event-to-document mapping.
challenges.alternative: Treat the signature as the start of a billing schedule: the contract carries its billing rules (one-off, milestones, recurring, deposit plus balance) and invoices are generated from that schedule, with the signature only activating it.

challenges.recommendation: Before build, list the real contract types and how each is billed, and agree where the billing rules live.

challenges.headline: Issue straight away, no review
challenges.premise: The system should create the invoice automatically, with nothing said about whether it is a draft or an issued document.
challenges.alternative: Create the invoice as a draft by default, with a validation step by finance. Issuing, which consumes a legal number and reaches the client, becomes a separate, deliberate act that can be automated later per client once the data proves reliable.
challenges.consequence: Issuing automatically on a signature with incomplete or wrong data creates legal documents with numbers in the gap-free sequence, and correcting them means credit notes rather than edits.
challenges.recommendation: Start with draft creation and an alert, and make auto-issue a later option once error rates are known.

challenges.headline: Build before checking what exists
challenges.premise: A new automation must be built to close the gap between signature and invoice.
challenges.alternative: First check whether the invoicing module, an accounting tool or an existing rule can already generate invoices from contracts, so that only a trigger needs wiring.
challenges.consequence: Building a generation engine where a feature is already licensed or switched off wastes effort and creates a second path to maintain.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm how invoices are produced today and whether any existing automation or downstream billing tool could be used.

complexity_reasons: French gap-free numbering and VAT rules
behaviour that may vary per client
briefs.cost_driver: deriving correct invoice content (amount, VAT, terms, schedule) from contract data
risks: Duplicate or wrong invoices from a re-fired signature event or a re-signed amendment.
A gap or misuse of the legal numbering sequence if invoices are issued then cancelled.
Incomplete contract data (amount, billing contact, VAT info) producing unusable invoices.
The shared approval and permission rules may need extending for who can see, edit or cancel generated invoices.
Per-client variation, if confirmed, multiplies configuration and testing.

opportunities.text: Build the contract-signed subscriber as a reusable event-to-action mechanism that other downstream automations can share.
Store billing rules on the contract (a billing schedule) so that manual and automatic invoicing draw from the same source.
Reuse contact roles (billing contact) to route notifications about generated invoices.

next_steps: Run a short discovery with finance: how invoices are produced today, which contract types exist and how each is billed, and what already exists that could be reused.
Decide the initial invoice status (draft with review, or issued) and the policy for incomplete contract data.
Build a first slice for the simplest contract type: draft creation, duplicate protection, link to the contract, and a notification to the billing contact.
Pilot with one or two clients before extending to other contract types and clients.

page.title: Automatic invoicing on contract signature
page.recommendation: Decide what a signature should produce before anything is built. We recommend starting with draft invoices created automatically on signature for your simplest contract type, reviewed by finance, and extending to other contract types and automatic issuing once the results are reliable.
page.why: You asked for an invoice to be created when a contract is signed. A contract often leads to several invoices, and an issued invoice takes a legal number and reaches the client, so errors are costly to undo. A draft-first approach delivers the time saving while keeping a human check on the first documents.
page.cost_and_risk: The main cost is working out the invoice content correctly (amount, VAT, terms, schedule) from the contract, rather than the trigger itself. The risk that matters most is a wrong or duplicate invoice, or a gap in the legal numbering sequence.

open.question: Does a signed contract lead to one invoice or several (milestones, recurring, deposit plus balance), and where do the amount, VAT, terms and currency come from?
open.would_change: Several invoices means building a billing schedule, which raises the effort considerably compared with one invoice.

open.question: How are invoices produced today, and does a tool or feature already in place (including in the invoicing module or accounting) cover this?
open.would_change: If something existing can do it, we would wire it up instead of building a new generator.

open.question: What is the underlying goal of this automation: fewer forgotten or late invoices, less manual work, or faster cash collection, and how would you know it worked?
open.would_change: If the goal is completeness rather than speed, we would prioritise a check that no signed contract is left without an invoice over fast issuing.

open.question: Should the invoice be a draft someone reviews, or issued and sent at once, and who reviews?
open.would_change: Immediate issuing removes the review step but requires much stricter data checks and numbering safeguards.

open.question: Is the behaviour the same for all clients, or does it vary by client, contract type or country?
open.would_change: Per-client variation requires a configuration layer and multiplies build and testing.

open.question: Who can see, edit or cancel a generated invoice, and who is notified?
open.would_change: It determines whether the permission rules and notification routing must be extended.

open.question: What should happen with amendments, duplicate signals, contracts cancelled after signature, and contracts signed before go-live?
open.would_change: It decides duplicate protection, amendment handling and whether a backfill is part of the scope.

assumptions.text: Invoices are created by hand today after signature, causing delays or forgotten invoices.
Generated invoices must follow French legal numbering and VAT rules.
This is an internal feature of the existing platform, not a new product.
Draft-first with finance review is the right starting status.

briefs.problem: Invoicing after a contract is signed is presumably manual, so it is slow, forgotten or error-prone. The client has not yet said what actually goes wrong.
briefs.solution: A link between the existing Contracts and Invoicing modules: when a contract is signed, the system prepares a correctly sourced, legally numbered invoice for review.
introduces: an event-driven automation that reacts to contract signature
a billing-rule layer that supplies amount, payment terms, VAT and currency to the invoice
idempotency protection so one signature never yields duplicate legally numbered invoices
an incomplete-data handling path with a visible pending or exception state
notification routing based on the client contact's role
handling of amendment signatures and signature cancellation

challenges.headline: Issue automatically, not draft first
challenges.premise: The request says an invoice is 'created automatically', which can be read as issued and sent without a human check.
challenges.alternative: Creating the invoice as a draft that billing reviews and issues keeps the automation but leaves the legal numbering step under human control. Direct issuance can be switched on later for contract types where the data has proven reliable.
challenges.consequence: An issued invoice takes a number from a gapless legal sequence and cannot be freely edited. A wrong or duplicate one sent to a client means credit notes and a damaged relationship.
challenges.recommendation: Start with draft creation plus a notification to billing, and decide on direct issuance only after the first clients have run it.

challenges.headline: Signature as the billing trigger
challenges.premise: Signature is taken to be the right moment to invoice, and one contract is taken to mean one invoice.
challenges.alternative: A contract can have several invoices (milestones, recurring, partial billing). Tying invoice creation to a billing schedule or start date, with signature only setting it up, avoids invoicing before the work begins.
challenges.consequence: Invoicing at signature for contracts that start later, or bill in stages, produces wrong invoices that must be cancelled or credited when deals change.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with Finance which billing pattern each contract type follows before fixing the trigger.

challenges.headline: Build before checking the need
challenges.premise: The request is a solution (an automatic invoice). Neither the actual pain nor today's process has been described.
challenges.alternative: If the pain is forgotten invoices, a reminder or a list of signed contracts without an invoice may solve it at a fraction of the cost. If it is slowness or errors, automation is justified.
challenges.consequence: Building a full automation for an unnamed problem risks solving the wrong thing and having no way to measure success.
challenges.recommendation: Have the client describe how invoicing is done today and what goes wrong, and agree one measure of success.

complexity_reasons: the invoice's amount, VAT, numbering and payment terms must all be sourced
idempotency and incomplete-data handling on an automatic trigger
briefs.cost_driver: the billing-rule logic that determines what each invoice contains
risks: Duplicate or wrong invoices consuming numbers from the legal gapless sequence.
An amendment signature re-triggering the automation and billing the same work twice.
Contracts signed with missing amount, billing contact or payment terms producing bad invoices or silent failures.
Invoices reaching clients by mistake if the review step is skipped.
Contracts signed before go-live being missed or billed twice if the backfill is not decided.

opportunities.text: Expose contract signature as a reusable event that other modules can subscribe to, rather than a one-off hook into invoicing.
Model billing rules (amount source, schedule, terms) as data attached to the contract or client, so milestone and recurring billing can be added later without a rewrite.
Reuse the existing role-based notification and approval mechanisms for the review of auto-created invoices.

next_steps: Run a short session with Finance and billing to establish how invoices are created today, what goes wrong, and one success measure.
Settle the billing pattern per contract type: one or several invoices, and where amount, VAT and payment terms come from.
Build the first version as a draft-creating automation with idempotency, incomplete-data alerts and billing notification.
Roll out to one pilot client or contract type behind a switch before widening.

decisions.decision: Extend the existing Contracts and Invoicing modules rather than buy or build a separate tool.
decisions.why: Both modules already exist, and the request names no external tool or budget.
decisions.alternative: An external billing or accounting tool.
decisions.tradeoff: Reuse is cheaper, but the platform must supply the billing rules itself.

decisions.decision: Automatic invoices are created as drafts for review, not issued directly, at launch.
decisions.why: Legal numbering and VAT make a wrong issued invoice costly to undo.
decisions.alternative: Direct issuance and sending on signature.
decisions.tradeoff: One review step remains, in exchange for much lower compliance and client-facing risk.

decisions.decision: Invoices must follow French VAT and gapless legal numbering.

exclusions.option: Retroactive invoicing of contracts signed before go-live
exclusions.reason: The scope of past contracts is unknown and a backfill risks duplicate or wrong legal invoices; it should follow once the automation is proven on new signatures.

exclusions.option: Fully configurable per-client billing rule engine in the first release
exclusions.reason: Whether behaviour really varies by client is unconfirmed, and no deadline or budget justifies a general engine before a pilot proves the need.

page.title: Automatic invoicing on signature: draft first
page.recommendation: Decide whether signing a contract should issue an invoice outright or prepare one for review. We recommend extending your existing Contracts and Invoicing modules so that a signature creates a draft invoice, notifies billing, and leaves issuance to a person at launch.
page.why: Both modules already exist, so this is a link between them rather than a new system. Invoices carry legal numbering and French VAT, which makes a wrong or duplicate issued invoice expensive to reverse. A draft step keeps most of the time saving while keeping that risk under control, and it can be relaxed once the automation has proven reliable.
page.cost_and_risk: The main effort is defining what goes into each invoice: where the amount, VAT, payment terms and billing contact come from, and whether one contract means one invoice or several. The risk that matters most is duplicate or wrong invoices, notably when an amendment is signed or a contract is signed with incomplete billing data.

open.question: Does one signed contract produce one invoice, or several (milestones, recurring, upfront)? And does the amount come from the contract or from a billing rule on the client?
open.would_change: If invoices are staged or recurring, this becomes a billing schedule feature and is substantially larger than a simple link.

open.question: How is invoicing done today and what exactly goes wrong: delays, forgotten invoices or errors?
open.would_change: If the pain is only forgotten invoices, a reminder or a list of uninvoiced signed contracts may be enough and the automation could be deferred.

open.question: Does this apply to every contract, client and country, and should each client be able to switch it on or off?
open.would_change: If behaviour varies by client, a configuration layer is needed and the build grows.

open.question: Who may see, edit or cancel an auto-created invoice, and who is notified?
open.would_change: Restricted rights or contact-role routing would extend the existing permission and notification framework.

open.question: Should a signed amendment, or a cancelled signature, create, adjust or cancel an invoice?
open.would_change: If yes, the automation needs versioned and reversal flows, not just a single creation step.

open.question: Does any unused billing capability or external accounting tool already exist, and should past signed contracts be invoiced retroactively?
open.would_change: Existing capability could shrink the build, while a backfill adds a separate migration scope.

assumptions.text: The signature of a contract is an existing event that other modules can listen to.
Existing modules are extended; nothing is bought or built from scratch, and no deadline or budget applies.
Invoices are created as drafts for review at launch.
Today the invoice is created by hand after signature.
